content: Nonpathogenic intestinal amebae infections occur when a person ingests contaminated substances, such as food or water, or touches contaminated surfaces and subsequently places their fingers in their mouth. The contamination originates from stool of an infected individual. Once inside the body, these parasites can persist for weeks, months, or even years. However, they remain confined to the intestines and do not spread to other parts of the body. The nonpathogenic species of intestinal amebae, including Chilomastix mesnili, Endolimax nana, Entamoeba coli, Entamoeba dispar, Entamoeba hartmanni, Entamoeba polecki, and Iodamoeba buetschlii, are distributed globally. Consequently, infections caused by these species are also observed worldwide. Notably, Entamoeba polecki is primarily a parasite of pigs and monkeys in natural settings, and human infections are more common in regions where close contact with animals occurs. The diagnosis of nonpathogenic intestinal amebae infections is made by identifying cysts and/or trophozoites in stool specimens. This is achieved through examination of concentrated wet mounts and permanent stained smears. While these species are generally considered nonpathogenic, they have been detected in the stool of patients presenting with diarrhea when no other known pathogens were identified. Their presence in stool may indicate fecal contamination of food or water sources and does not exclude the possibility of other parasitic infections. Additionally, Entamoeba gingivalis, another nonpathogenic species, is found in approximately 95% of patients with gum disease and about 50% of individuals with healthy gums. Currently, there are no treatment recommendations for these six species, as they are generally regarded as nonpathogenic.
